title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
ru: Молодой учёный создаёт живое существо, отвергает его — и чудовище, жаждущее любви, начинает мстить создателю

chapters.title: Chapter 1. Letters from the Ice
chapters.text:
St. Petersburg, December. My dear sister Margaret, you will be glad to hear that I have arrived safely and that my great journey has finally begun. You always worried about this plan of mine, but I cannot give it up. Since I was a boy I have dreamed of sailing into the frozen seas of the North, where no one has ever been. Perhaps I will find a passage through the ice. Perhaps I will discover the secret of the magnet that makes the compass needle point north. Whatever happens, I will have done something that nobody has done before.

I have hired a ship and a crew of brave, experienced sailors. Only one thing is missing: a friend. I have no one on board who shares my dreams, no one with whom I can talk about books and ideas. Sometimes I feel very lonely, Margaret.

Some months later, on the ice. My dear sister, something so strange has happened that I must write it down at once. Our ship has been trapped by ice for several days, and thick fog surrounds us. Yesterday, when the fog lifted a little, we saw a sledge pulled by dogs, moving quickly across the ice about half a mile away. The driver looked like a man, but he was enormous, far larger than any human being. He disappeared among the distant hills of ice, and we stared after him in silence.

The next morning the ice broke up around us, and a piece of it floated close to the ship. On it lay another sledge, with only one living dog, and a man who was almost frozen to death. This man was not a giant. He was thin and pale, and his eyes were full of pain. When my sailors invited him on board, he first asked, “Where is your ship going?” Only when I told him that we were sailing north did he agree to come with us.

We carried him down to my cabin, rubbed his cold body with brandy and gave him soup. It was two days before he could speak properly. When one of my officers asked him why he had travelled so far across the ice, his face darkened. “To find someone who is running from me,” he answered.

“Was he travelling on a sledge, like yours?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Then I think we saw him, the day before we found you.”

The stranger became very excited and asked me many questions about the direction the giant had taken. After that he was quiet for a long time.

Over the following weeks, as his health slowly returned, I came to love this man like a brother. He is gentle and wise, and when he talks about nature or poetry his whole face lights up. Yet a terrible sadness is always with him. One evening I told him about my own ambitions: how I would give anything, even my life, to gain new knowledge for mankind. He listened with a look of horror.

“Unhappy man!” he cried. “Do you share my madness? Listen to my story, and perhaps it will stop you before it is too late.”

He told me his name was Victor Frankenstein. The next day he began his story, and every night I have written down what he said, as closely as I can remember it. This is his story, Margaret, told in his own words.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. A Childhood in Geneva
chapters.text:
“I was born in Geneva, into one of the most respected families of the city. My father, Alphonse Frankenstein, was an honest and much-admired man who had served his country for many years. He married late, and my mother was the daughter of an old friend of his who had died in poverty. They loved each other deeply, and I was their first child, their toy and their treasure.

When I was about five years old, my mother visited a poor family on the shores of Lake Como in Italy. Among their dark-haired children she noticed a little girl with golden hair and blue eyes, who seemed quite different from the others. She learned that the child was an orphan, the daughter of a nobleman from Milan. My mother asked if she could take her home, and so Elizabeth Lavenza came to live with us. My mother told me that Elizabeth was a present for me, and I believed it. From that day we grew up together, not quite as brother and sister, but as something closer than friends.

Later my parents had two more sons, Ernest and little William. My closest companion outside the family was Henry Clerval, the son of a merchant. Henry loved stories of knights and adventure, while I was hungry for another kind of knowledge. I wanted to learn the secrets of heaven and earth, the hidden laws of nature.

When I was thirteen, I found a book by Cornelius Agrippa, an old alchemist, and read it with enthusiasm. My father glanced at it and said it was rubbish, but he did not explain why. If he had, I might have thrown it away. Instead I read everything I could find by the old alchemists, who had searched for the elixir of life and the philosopher's stone. I dreamed of banishing disease and making man safe from every death except a violent one.

Then, when I was fifteen, I watched a violent thunderstorm from our house near the lake. A bolt of lightning struck an old oak tree, and when the light disappeared, the tree had been reduced to a blasted stump. A visitor explained the theory of electricity to me, and my old heroes suddenly seemed foolish. For a while I gave up science altogether. Now I believe that this was the last effort of my guardian angel to save me.

When I was seventeen, my parents decided that I should study at the University of Ingolstadt in Germany. But before I left, the first misfortune of my life took place. Elizabeth caught scarlet fever. My mother nursed her day and night, and Elizabeth recovered, but my mother caught the illness herself. On her deathbed she joined Elizabeth's hands and mine. “My children,” she said, “my firmest hopes of future happiness were placed on your union. Elizabeth, my love, you must take my place with the younger children.” She died calmly, and for a long time our home was filled with grief.

A few weeks later I set off for Ingolstadt. Henry came to say goodbye; his father had refused to let him go to university, and he watched my carriage leave with sad eyes. I was alone for the first time in my life, and I was entering a world of strangers.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Secret of Life
chapters.text:
“At Ingolstadt I met two professors. The first, Krempe, laughed at me when I mentioned the alchemists. ‘You have wasted your time on nonsense,’ he said. The second, Professor Waldman, was a kind man with a gentle voice. In his first lecture he explained that the ancient teachers had promised impossible things, while modern scientists promised very little but actually performed miracles. ‘They have discovered how the blood circulates and what the air we breathe is made of,’ he said. ‘They can command the thunders of heaven.’

His words changed my life. ‘So much has been done,’ I said to myself, ‘but I will achieve more. I will explore unknown powers and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.’

For two years I worked with such passion that I hardly left the laboratory. I made discoveries that impressed even my professors. But one question fascinated me more than any other: where does life come from? To examine the causes of life, I had first to study death. I spent long nights in places where the dead are kept, observing how the body changes and decays. I was never afraid; I thought only of my work.

Then, after days and nights of incredible labour, I made a discovery so great and so simple that I was amazed no one had found it before me. I had learned how to give life to lifeless matter.

Do not ask me how, my friend. I will not tell you. Learn from my example how dangerous knowledge is, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world.

I decided to create a human being. Because the smaller parts of the body were so difficult to work with, I made my creature very large, about eight feet tall. I collected materials in secret, working in a lonely room at the top of the house. I forgot my family and my friends. I did not notice the seasons change. I became thin and pale, and my nerves were so weak that a falling leaf frightened me.

At last, on a dreary night in November, I saw the result of my efforts. It was one o'clock in the morning; the rain was beating against the window and my candle had almost burnt out. By its dim light I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open. It breathed hard, and its arms and legs moved.

How can I describe my feelings? I had chosen its features to be beautiful. Beautiful! Its yellow skin hardly covered the muscles beneath; its hair was long and black and its teeth were white as pearls, but these only made a more horrible contrast with its watery eyes and its thin black lips. The beauty of my dream vanished, and my heart filled with horror and disgust.

I rushed out of the room and threw myself on my bed. When I finally slept, I had terrible dreams. I woke in a cold sweat and saw the creature standing by my bed, holding up the curtain. His eyes were fixed on me. He made some sounds and smiled, and he stretched out a hand, perhaps to stop me. But I escaped and ran downstairs, and I spent the rest of the night walking in the courtyard.

In the morning, as I wandered through the streets, a coach stopped beside me, and out jumped Henry Clerval! His father had finally allowed him to study. I was overjoyed, but when we reached my rooms, I was terrified that the monster would be there. The room was empty. I laughed wildly, and then I collapsed. For several months I lay ill with a nervous fever, and Henry nursed me with endless patience.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Death of William
chapters.text:
“By spring I had recovered. I could not bear to see my scientific instruments, and I studied languages with Henry instead. I was almost happy again. Then a letter arrived from my father.

‘William is dead!’ he wrote. ‘That sweet child, whose smiles delighted all of us, has been murdered. Last Thursday we went for a walk outside the city. William and Ernest ran ahead, and in the evening we could not find William. At dawn we discovered him lying on the grass. The murderer's finger was marked on his neck. Elizabeth is in despair. She had let him wear a little picture of your mother, and it is gone; she believes it was the reason for the crime. Come home, Victor. Only you can comfort her.’

I left Ingolstadt at once. It was night when I arrived near Geneva, and the city gates were already shut, so I walked to the place where William had died. A storm broke over the mountains, and the lightning lit up the lake. Suddenly, in a flash of light, I saw a figure among the trees. Its huge size and its unnatural face told me immediately who it was: the creature I had made. Then I understood. He was the murderer of my brother! I could not doubt it. The figure climbed the steep rocks with impossible speed and disappeared.

I could have told the police, but who would believe me? They would think I was mad. So I said nothing, and my silence became the second great crime of my life.

At home I discovered that someone had been arrested for the murder. It was Justine Moritz, a gentle girl who had lived with our family for years and loved William as if he were her own. The picture of my mother had been found in the pocket of her dress.

‘She is innocent!’ I cried. ‘I know who the murderer is.’

Elizabeth agreed with me. ‘I know her,’ she said. ‘She could never do such a thing.’

At the trial, Justine explained that she had been out searching for William all night. When the city gates were closed, she had slept in a barn. She had no idea how the picture had got into her pocket. Elizabeth spoke bravely in her defence, but the evidence was against her. Worse, a priest had frightened her so much that she had confessed, hoping to be forgiven by the church. Later she told Elizabeth and me the truth. ‘I confessed a lie,’ she said, ‘and now it weighs on my soul more than all my other sins.’

Justine was condemned and executed. I, the true cause of these deaths, had to stand by and watch. I wanted to confess everything, but I knew that no one would believe my story. Two innocent people had died because of me, and I felt as if I carried a hell inside me that nothing could put out.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Meeting on the Glacier
chapters.text:
“After Justine's death I could find no peace. I avoided my family and spent hours alone in a boat on the lake, sometimes tempted to throw myself into the water and end my suffering. Only the thought of Elizabeth and my father stopped me. I was also afraid that the monster would do something new, and I wanted to be there to protect them.

At last I decided to travel into the mountains. I had always loved the Alps, and I hoped that their wild beauty would calm my mind. I went up to the valley of Chamonix, and one morning I climbed alone to the great glacier called the Mer de Glace, the Sea of Ice. The view from the top was magnificent: the river of ice stretched out below me, and the white peaks shone above the clouds. For a moment my heart felt lighter.

Suddenly I saw a figure moving towards me across the ice at superhuman speed. It was the creature. I trembled with rage and horror.

‘Devil!’ I shouted. ‘Do you dare to come near me? Go away, or let me destroy you!’

‘I expected this reception,’ said the creature calmly. ‘All men hate the wretched, and I am more wretched than any living thing. Yet you, my creator, hate me too, though we are bound together until one of us dies. You want to kill me. How can you play with life like this? Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind.’

I rushed at him, but he easily avoided me. ‘Be calm,’ he said. ‘I have suffered enough already. Remember that you made me stronger than yourself, but I will not fight you. I am your creature, and I would be gentle and obedient to you if you would only do your part. Remember, I ought to be your Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom you drive from joy for no crime. Everywhere I see happiness from which I alone am excluded. I was kind and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.’

‘Go away!’ I said. ‘I will not listen to you. We are enemies.’

‘How can I move you?’ he said. ‘Believe me, Frankenstein, I was full of love, but I have been alone and hated. These icy caves are the only home I have, because man does not hate them. Listen to my story. When you have heard it, you can abandon me or feel pity for me, as you judge that I deserve. But hear me first. The murderer is allowed to speak before he is condemned. You accuse me of murder, and yet you would kill your own creature with a satisfied conscience.’

His words made me think. For the first time, I felt that a creator had duties towards the being he had made. It started to rain, and he led me to a hut on the mountain. There, sitting by a fire he had made, the creature began his tale.”

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Creature’s Story
chapters.text:
“‘I can hardly remember the first days of my existence,’ he said. ‘Light, darkness, heat and cold confused me. When I left your rooms, I found a coat and walked into the forest near Ingolstadt. I was hungry and thirsty, and I ate berries and drank from streams. One night I discovered a fire left by some travellers. I put my hand into it and pulled it out with a cry; how strange that the same thing could give such warmth and such pain!

Soon I discovered what men thought of me. I entered a village, and the moment the people saw me, children screamed and women fainted. Men attacked me with stones and sticks until I escaped into the fields. After that I hid in a small shed attached to a cottage in the woods. Through a crack in the wall I could see into the cottage, and for many months I watched the family who lived there.

There was an old man, who was blind and who played beautiful music on a guitar. There was a young man called Felix and his sister Agatha. They were very poor, and sometimes the young people went without food so that the old man could eat. I had been stealing some of their vegetables, but when I saw this, I stopped. Instead, at night, I collected firewood and left it by their door. In the morning they were amazed, and they spoke of a good spirit who was helping them. It made me happy to hear it.

I noticed that these people communicated through sounds that made them smile or become sad. I wanted to learn this godlike science. Slowly I learned the words for fire, milk and bread, and the names of the family. Then a beautiful young woman arrived, called Safie. She was a foreigner, and Felix loved her. Because she did not speak their language, Felix taught her, and I learned together with her through the crack in the wall. I learned to speak, and then to read.

From their conversations I learned their history. The old man was called De Lacey. They had once been a rich family in Paris, but Felix had helped Safie's father escape from prison, and as a punishment they had lost their fortune and had been sent into exile.

I also found some books in the forest: Paradise Lost, a volume of Plutarch's Lives and The Sorrows of Young Werther. They taught me about gods and heroes, love and death. And in the pocket of my coat I found your journal, Frankenstein. I read how you had created me, and how you had turned away in disgust. Cursed creator! Why did you form a monster so hideous that even you turned from me? Satan had his companions, but I am solitary and hated.

One day I saw my own face reflected in a pool, and I jumped back in horror. At last I understood why people ran from me. Still, I hoped that these good cottagers would see past my appearance and love me for my kindness. Since the old man was blind, I decided to speak to him first, while the others were out.’”

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Fire and Revenge
chapters.text:
“‘I knocked at the door,’ the creature continued. ‘The old man welcomed me kindly and asked me to sit by the fire. I told him that I was a traveller in need of friends, and that the people I loved had a prejudice against me because they had never really looked at my heart. “I am blind,” he said, “and cannot judge your face, but there is something in your words which tells me that you are sincere.”

At that moment Felix, Agatha and Safie came in. When they saw me, Agatha fainted and Safie ran out of the cottage. Felix pulled me away from his father and struck me violently with a stick. I could have torn him apart, but my heart was sick, and I ran back to my shed. A few days later the family left the cottage for ever. They were so afraid of me that they never came back.

That night I declared war on the whole human race, and above all on you, who had given me life and then left me to this misery. I set fire to the empty cottage and watched it burn. Then, since I knew from your journal where your family lived, I travelled towards Geneva.

On the way, something happened that confirmed my hatred. I saw a young girl slip into a fast river, and I jumped in and pulled her out. As I was trying to bring her back to life, a man came running up. He took the girl from my arms, and when I followed, he shot me. The bullet entered my shoulder. This was the reward for my kindness!

When I finally reached the woods near Geneva, a small boy ran into the place where I was hiding. I thought that a child might be too young to have learned to hate. If I could make him my friend, I would not be so lonely. I caught hold of him, but he screamed and called me an ogre. “My papa is Monsieur Frankenstein,” he shouted, “and he will punish you!”

Frankenstein! You belong to my enemy. I held him to make him silent, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet. I felt a hellish joy. Around his neck I saw a picture of a lovely woman. Later I found a young woman sleeping in a barn, and I put the picture in the pocket of her dress. She, too, would suffer for the crime, since I was never allowed to know the love of such a woman.

Now listen to my demand. I am alone. You must create a female for me, a companion as ugly as I am, with whom I can live. We will go to the wild places of South America and never be seen by men again. We will eat acorns and berries, and the sun will shine on us as it shines on man. If I have someone to love, my evil passions will disappear. If you refuse, I will destroy you and everyone you love.’

I was torn between pity and horror. At last I said, ‘I agree to your demand, on condition that you leave Europe for ever with your companion.’

‘I swear it,’ he said. ‘Go to your work. I shall watch its progress with unspeakable anxiety.’ Then he left me and climbed down the mountain faster than an eagle.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The Broken Promise
chapters.text:
“When I returned home, my father noticed my sadness. He asked me gently whether I wished to marry Elizabeth, as my mother had wanted. I loved her with all my heart, but I could not marry her while this terrible task lay before me. I told him that I first needed to travel to England, where I could learn about recent scientific discoveries. In truth, I did not want to perform such work in my family's house.

Henry Clerval came with me. We travelled down the Rhine and then to London, Oxford and the lakes of Cumberland. Henry enjoyed every hill and every old castle, while I felt like a criminal hiding a dreadful secret. At last I left him in Scotland, promising to join him later, and I went to one of the most remote islands of the Orkneys. There, in a poor hut beside the grey sea, I began to create the second being.

It was a horrible labour. As I worked, I began to think about what I was doing. This female might become ten thousand times more evil than her mate. She had not made any promise; perhaps she would refuse to go into the wilderness with him. Perhaps they would hate each other. And even if they lived together in peace, they might have children, and a race of devils would spread upon the earth. Had I the right to buy my own peace at the price of the whole human race?

One night, as I sat thinking, I looked up and saw the creature's face at the window. He was grinning. He had followed me all the way to watch my work. Trembling with passion, I tore the half-finished body to pieces in front of his eyes. He gave a howl of despair and disappeared.

Later he came to the door. ‘You have destroyed the work which you began,’ he said. ‘Do you dare to break your promise? Slave, you are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!’

‘Never,’ I answered. ‘I will not create another like you.’

‘Then I shall go,’ he said, ‘but remember: I shall be with you on your wedding-night.’

I thought that he intended to kill me on that night, and strangely, I was not afraid for myself. I only thought of Elizabeth's tears when she learned of my death.

A few days later I took the remains of my work in a basket, rowed out to sea and threw them into the water. Afterwards I fell asleep in the boat, and the wind carried me far away. When I finally reached land, I found myself in a small town in Ireland. The people there looked at me with suspicion, and I was taken to a magistrate, Mr Kirwin. A young man had been found dead on the beach the night before, with the marks of fingers on his neck.

They took me to see the body. It was Henry Clerval. I threw myself on his body and cried, ‘Have my murderous plans deprived you also, my dearest Henry, of life?’ Then I collapsed and fell into a fever that lasted two months.”

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Wedding Night
chapters.text:
“When I recovered, I was in prison. Mr Kirwin had been kind to me; he had even written to my father, who arrived to comfort me. Witnesses proved that I had been on the Orkney Islands when Henry was killed, and I was released. But I felt no joy. ‘I am the murderer of William, of Justine, and of Henry,’ I said to my father, who thought that my illness had disturbed my mind.

On the journey home I received a letter from Elizabeth. She had noticed my strange behaviour, and she asked whether I loved another woman. If so, she wrote, I should feel free. I answered that I loved only her, and that we would marry as soon as I came home. I also promised to tell her a terrible secret on the day after our wedding.

I remembered the monster's words, ‘I shall be with you on your wedding-night.’ Very well, I thought. On that night the fight between us would end, one way or the other. I carried pistols and a dagger at all times and watched every shadow.

We were married in Geneva, and in the afternoon we set off by boat across the lake to spend our first night at an inn at Evian. The sun was shining, the mountains were beautiful, and for a few hours Elizabeth was happy. She took my hand and said, ‘Why are you so sad, my love? Look how peaceful everything is.’ But when evening came, the wind rose, and my fears returned.

At the inn I asked Elizabeth to go to bed, while I walked through the passages of the house with my pistol, searching for my enemy. Suddenly I heard a dreadful scream from our room. In that moment I understood everything. The monster had never intended to kill me on my wedding-night. He wanted me to live, and to suffer as he suffered.

I rushed into the room. Elizabeth lay across the bed, lifeless, her face pale. I fell down beside her. When I looked up, I saw at the open window the most hateful face in the world. The monster was grinning and pointing at the body of my wife. I fired my pistol, but he escaped, running with the speed of lightning, and plunged into the lake.

Men searched for him for hours, but they found nothing. I returned to Geneva with the terrible news. My father could not bear the loss of Elizabeth, whom he had loved as his own daughter. A few days later he died in my arms.

For a long time afterwards I was out of my mind, and they shut me in a cell. When my reason returned, I went to a magistrate and told him the whole story. He listened politely, but I could see that he did not really believe me, and that he would do nothing. Then I knew what I must do. I would hunt the monster down myself, and I would not rest until one of us was dead.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10. The End of the Chase
chapters.text:
“Before I left Geneva for ever, I went to the cemetery where William, Elizabeth and my father lay. I knelt on the grass and swore to pursue the creature until I destroyed him. In the silence of the night I heard a loud laugh, and a well-known voice whispered near my ear: ‘I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied.’

I have followed him ever since. I followed him along the Rhône, across the Mediterranean, through the wilds of Tartary and Russia. Sometimes he left messages carved on trees or stones: ‘My reign is not yet over. Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, to which I am unaffected.’ Sometimes he even left food for me, so that I would not die and end the game too soon. When the snow came, I bought a sledge and dogs, and I followed him onto the frozen sea. I was only a mile behind him when the ice broke, and I was carried away on a floating piece of it. Then your ship found me.

Walton, if I die, promise me that you will not let him live. Swear that he will not triumph over my misery!”

Here Victor's story ends, Margaret. He showed me letters from Felix and Safie which the creature had given him, and I cannot doubt that every word is true.

Our situation is now very dangerous. The ship is surrounded by mountains of ice, and some of my men have died of cold. The crew came to me and asked me to promise that, if the ice opened, we would turn south and go home. Before I could answer, Victor raised himself from his bed. “Are you such cowards?” he cried. “You wanted glory and danger! Be men, or be more than men.” His words moved them, but in the end I agreed. When the ice broke, we turned towards England. I have lost my dream, Margaret, but I shall bring my men home alive.

Victor grew weaker every day. On his last evening he took my hand. “Seek happiness in tranquillity,” he said, “and avoid ambition, even the apparently innocent ambition of distinguishing yourself in science. Yet why do I say this? I have myself been blasted in these hopes, yet another may succeed.” His voice became fainter, and a gentle smile crossed his face. Then he was gone.

At midnight I heard a strange voice in the cabin. I went in and saw a gigantic figure bending over Victor's body. When he heard me, he turned to leave, but I asked him to stay.

“That is also my victim,” he said. “Do not think that I felt no pain. My heart was made for love and sympathy, and when misery turned it towards hatred, the change hurt me more than you can imagine. After the death of Clerval I pitied Frankenstein. But when I learned that he hoped for happiness while I was alone, I was filled with envy and rage.”

“And now that he is dead,” I said, “do you feel sorry?”

“I am the only one who does,” he answered. “He suffered, but I suffered more. Fear not that I shall do more harm. My work is nearly complete. I shall go to the farthest north, build my funeral pile and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that no one will ever be able to make another like me. Farewell!”

With these words he jumped from the cabin window onto an ice raft that lay close to the ship. He was soon carried away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.
